paragraphs: When several language-model agents collaborate, a majority vote can make agreement look stronger than it is. Agents may choose the same answer while retaining contradictory beliefs, leaving their consensus unstable. This paper also questions whether every agent should interact equally with every other agent, since some collaborators may be more useful for achieving stable agreement.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for choosing collaborators that maximize consensus stability. Their Belief-Calibrated Consensus Seeking framework, BCCS, uses this analysis to select collaboration partners and assess agreement using the system's internal beliefs. Partner selection and consensus assessment therefore work together: the method changes both whom agents consult and how their resulting agreement is judged.

Experiments on MATH and MMLU report accuracy improvements of 2.23% and 3.95%, respectively, over the best existing results. These findings support the value of considering the structure of collaboration and underlying beliefs when coordinating agents on challenging tasks. The contribution connects a theoretical account of stable consensus with empirical improvements in answer accuracy.
neurips-2025-belief-calibrated-multi-age.tldr: BCCS improves multi-agent collaboration by selecting partners for stable consensus and checking agreement against agents' internal beliefs.

paragraphs: Selecting a small set of informative variables can make a model easier to interpret and help it generalize. Modern mixed integer programming has made this selection practical for large non-private regression problems. This paper investigates how to bring those optimization advances into variable selection with differential privacy, introducing two private estimators.

The approach uses structured sampling procedures inspired by the exponential mechanism. Rather than exhaustively examining every possible feature subset, these procedures explore the non-convex objective using modern integer programming techniques. The framework accommodates objectives for both regression and classification. For best subset selection, the authors also provide theoretical guarantees about recovering the relevant variables, a property called support recovery.

Numerical experiments use least squares and hinge loss, testing settings with up to 10,000 variables. The methods achieve state-of-the-art empirical support recovery and outperform competing algorithms in those experiments. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: it connects private selection to practical optimization tools while supporting feature recovery through theory in the best subset setting and experiments across two objectives.
neurips-2025-differentially-private-high.tldr: Two private variable-selection methods use integer programming and structured sampling to recover informative features without exhaustive subset search.

paragraphs: A classifier can learn shortcuts when an incidental image attribute strongly correlates with the target label. Unsupervised debiasing methods may use an auxiliary model that deliberately captures this bias, helping the overall method address it. However, training that auxiliary model can go wrong when it memorizes examples that contradict the dominant shortcut.

Diffusing DeBias addresses this issue by using conditional diffusion models to generate images aligned with the bias. These synthetic images fully replace the original dataset specifically for training the auxiliary bias amplifier. The method deliberately uses diffusion models' tendency to reproduce biased patterns, turning that tendency into a component of the debiasing procedure.

The trained amplifier can be incorporated into both an end-to-end approach and a two-step unsupervised debiasing approach. Experiments report improvements over the state of the art on multiple benchmark datasets. The finding supports a targeted use of synthetic data: strengthening a shortcut in an auxiliary model can help debias the final model when it addresses the auxiliary model's memorization problem.
neurips-2025-diffusing-debias-synthetic-.tldr: Diffusing DeBias trains auxiliary bias models on synthetic shortcut-aligned images to improve unsupervised classifier debiasing.

paragraphs: Making endoscopic imaging smaller requires reducing the optics needed to capture useful images. Optical fibers offer a narrow imaging channel, but approaches based on scanning or bundles of fiber cores face limits in speed and resolution. This paper combines an optical measurement system with learned reconstruction to obtain images through a single-core fiber.

Optical frequency combs produce precise speckle illumination patterns in parallel using different wavelengths. Dual-comb ghost imaging then captures compressed, summed light measurements with a single-pixel detector. This snapshot measurement arrangement removes the need for spatial and spectral scanning. Because the measurements are highly compressed, reconstructing a detailed image becomes a central part of the system.

The authors introduce Optical Ghost-GPT, a transformer model that reconstructs images quickly and with high fidelity at low sampling rates. They report that the combined optical and computational approach exceeds classical ghost imaging in speed and accuracy, enabling real-time, high-resolution imaging with a smaller device footprint. The work points toward compact, lower-cost endomicroscopy and other sensing applications constrained by hardware size.
neurips-2025-dual-comb-ghost-imaging-wit.tldr: A single-core fiber imaging system combines parallel optical measurements with transformer reconstruction for fast, compact endomicroscopy.

paragraphs: Understanding an activity from the participant's viewpoint and from an outside observer's viewpoint requires connecting information across perspectives. A model that understands either video individually may still struggle to relate them. EgoExoBench creates a dedicated evaluation of this ability in multimodal large language models, focusing on first-person and third-person video understanding.

Built from publicly available datasets, the benchmark contains more than 7,300 question–answer pairs across eleven subtasks. These are organized around three challenges: aligning meaning across perspectives, associating viewpoints, and reasoning about time. This structure separates different demands of cross-view understanding rather than treating performance on individual videos as evidence that a model can integrate their perspectives.

The authors evaluate thirteen leading multimodal models. Although the models perform strongly on single-view tasks, they struggle with semantic alignment, view association, and temporal dynamics in the combined setting. The results identify a gap between understanding an isolated perspective and connecting perspectives. The benchmark is intended to support research on embodied agents and assistants that need this broader form of video understanding.
neurips-2025-egoexobench-a-benchmark-for.tldr: EgoExoBench reveals that strong single-view video understanding does not reliably translate into reasoning across first-person and third-person perspectives.

paragraphs: The Schrödinger Bridge problem is used in computational optimal transport and generative modeling. Iterative Markovian Fitting, or IMF, is an idealized method for solving it. Earlier theory established that IMF converges eventually, but did not quantify its progress after a finite number of iterations. This paper supplies such a quantitative convergence result.

The authors prove exponential convergence under structural assumptions on the reference measure and marginal distributions, with a sufficiently large time horizon. They cover two regimes: log-concave marginals and the broader case of weakly log-concave marginals. The guarantee therefore depends on these conditions; it is a statement about IMF in the analyzed settings rather than unrestricted convergence for every bridge problem.

The analysis develops new contraction results for the Markovian projection operator, providing the mathematical basis for controlling how the iteration progresses. This strengthens an eventual-convergence statement into a finite-iteration rate. The work also lays groundwork for analyzing Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge Matching, a practical approximation, while the stated exponential guarantees apply to IMF itself.
neurips-2025-exponential-convergence-gua.tldr: The paper proves finite-iteration exponential convergence for Iterative Markovian Fitting under structural assumptions and a sufficiently large time horizon.

paragraphs: Neural processes learn distributions over data-dependent functions, supporting prediction and sampling conditioned on observations. This paper introduces a neural process built using flow matching, a generative modeling approach. The objective is to predict conditional distributions at arbitrary requested points while retaining a straightforward procedure for drawing samples from those distributions.

The model follows the neural process training framework, so a trained model provides amortized conditional predictions across different sets of points. Sampling uses an ordinary differential equation solver without an additional conditioning method. This makes conditional generation part of the model's sampling procedure. The solver's number of steps also gives users a way to control the balance between prediction accuracy and running time.

The authors evaluate the method on synthetic one-dimensional Gaussian process data, two-dimensional images, and real weather data. They report better performance than previous state-of-the-art neural process methods across these benchmarks. Together, the results support flow matching as a useful foundation for neural processes, combining conditional sampling with an adjustable computational budget across several kinds of data.
neurips-2025-flow-matching-neural-proces.tldr: Flow Matching Neural Processes provide conditional sampling through an ODE solver with an adjustable accuracy–runtime tradeoff.

paragraphs: Top-k decoding samples a language model's next token after retaining only its k most probable options and rescaling their probabilities. It is often motivated by the idea that model probabilities contain noise and the desired distribution has relatively few plausible tokens. This paper gives that intuition a mathematical formulation based on recovering a sparse probability distribution.

The authors introduce Bregman decoders, which balance a divergence-based measure of distribution mismatch against a penalty for keeping more tokens. They study both primal and dual formulations. These decoders can adapt the number of retained tokens to the current distribution, giving an optimization-based way to choose k instead of fixing it across all token predictions.

For a large class of divergences, the authors prove that greedy strategies solve the selection problem and that the objective is discretely convex in k, enabling logarithmic-time identification of the optimal k. Standard top-k emerges from the KL-divergence case. Other choices produce different behavior, including nonlinear increases in the weight assigned to larger probabilities, broadening the available decoding strategies.
neurips-2025-foundations-of-top-k-decodi.tldr: A sparse-distribution optimization framework explains top-k decoding and yields efficient alternatives that adapt how many tokens they retain.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning models often explain their answers entirely in words, leaving the image regions they consult implicit. GRIT trains multimodal language models to combine written reasoning with explicit references to the input image. Its reasoning chains interleave text and bounding box coordinates, connecting steps in the explanation to particular visual regions.

The training method, GRPO-GR, builds on the GRPO reinforcement learning algorithm. Its rewards emphasize final-answer correctness and the required grounded reasoning format. This avoids requiring training examples annotated with complete reasoning chains or explicit bounding box labels. The model instead learns from image–question–answer triplets while being rewarded for producing answers and reasoning in the intended form.

The authors report that training can work with as few as twenty such triplets from existing datasets. Their evaluations show coherent reasoning chains that incorporate visual grounding, supporting the possibility of learning both abilities together with little annotated task data. The contribution is a training approach and output format that make visual references explicit within the reasoning process.
neurips-2025-grit-teaching-mllms-to-thin.tldr: GRIT uses reinforcement learning to teach multimodal models to interleave textual reasoning with image-region coordinates using sparse answer-level supervision.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn from changing data without forgetting earlier knowledge. Parameter-efficient approaches can freeze a pretrained model and train small sets of task-specific parameters without retaining historical examples. At prediction time, however, they must select the appropriate parameters. Matching based only on pretrained features can overlook knowledge acquired during task training.

HRM-PET uses the initial predicted distribution to reconsider this selection. Its direct re-matching mechanism handles cases where the prediction identifies the correct task despite an incorrect initial match. A second, confidence-based mechanism addresses more difficult mismatches that the direct mechanism cannot correct. Together, these steps use information from the trained parameters to improve how those parameters are retrieved.

The method also adds cross-task instance relationship distillation to learn task-invariant knowledge useful for matching. Experiments across four datasets and five pretrained settings show favorable performance against state-of-the-art methods. The results support improving the connection between task-specific learning and inference-time selection, making fuller use of knowledge already present in the tuned parameters.
neurips-2025-hybrid-re-matching-for-cont.tldr: HRM-PET improves continual learning by using predictions and confidence to reconsider which task-specific parameters should guide inference.

paragraphs: Compressing language models below one bit per weight creates a difficult tradeoff between storage and lost information. LittleBit targets extremely small representations, including 0.1 bits per weight. The abstract reports nearly 31-fold memory reduction and gives an example of compressing Llama2-13B to less than 0.9 GB.

LittleBit first represents weight matrices through low-rank latent factors, then binarizes those factors. Compensation operates across rows, columns, and latent dimensions, with the latent component learning the importance of individual ranks. Dual Sign-Value-Independent Decomposition initializes quantization-aware training, while integrated residual compensation reduces errors introduced by the compressed representation. These components address information loss at several levels of the factorization.

Experiments report that LittleBit at 0.1 bits per weight on Llama2-7B surpasses a leading method operating at 0.7 bits per weight. The paper also describes a potential 11.6-fold speedup over FP16 at the kernel level. These findings support a favorable size–performance tradeoff at extreme compression, while the speed claim remains specifically potential and kernel-level.
neurips-2025-littlebit-ultra-low-bit-qua.tldr: LittleBit combines binarized low-rank factors with learned compensation to compress language models to extremely low bits per weight.

paragraphs: Low-light enhancement must recover useful image detail while working across different lighting conditions. Methods trained as fixed mappings between paired dark and normally lit images can generalize poorly when reference images are unavailable. LASQ approaches enhancement through a statistical description of brightness transitions, motivated by empirical observations of power-law behavior in natural luminance changes.

The framework represents these transitions using hierarchical luminance distributions approximated by stratified power functions. Enhancement becomes probabilistic sampling across continuous brightness layers. A diffusion forward process discovers transition paths between the layers, allowing the method to emulate luminance distributions without normally lit reference images. This formulation makes the structure of brightness changes central to learning.

The authors report improved performance in practical settings without normal-light references. They also apply the framework when references are available, reporting superior performance on domain-specific datasets and better generalization across non-reference datasets. The contribution is a statistical alternative to deterministic pixel mappings, with reported benefits in both reference-based and reference-free enhancement settings.
neurips-2025-luminance-aware-statistical.tldr: LASQ models low-light enhancement as sampling across brightness distributions, enabling learning without normally lit reference images.

paragraphs: Whole-slide pathology classification must connect broad tissue appearance with small structures such as nuclei and glands. Prompt-based adaptation of vision-language models can reduce annotation needs, but slide-level prompts may overlook subtype-specific appearances of these structures. MAPLE introduces a hierarchy that learns from both individual histological entities and the slide as a whole.

The method uses language models to generate prompts describing entities, their phenotypic attributes, and global slide appearance. Entity-guided cross-attention extracts features, which are aligned with subtype-specific descriptions to make fine-grained predictions. A graph module then updates entity representations using semantic relationships within a scale and across different scales, connecting local evidence observed at different levels.

The refined entity features are aggregated into a slide representation and aligned with slide-level prompts. Final predictions combine the entity-level and slide-level outputs. Results on three cancer cohorts support the method's effectiveness for few-shot pathology classification. The approach matters because it makes detailed, subtype-relevant evidence contribute explicitly alongside the overall slide description when labeled examples are limited.
neurips-2025-maple-multi-scale-attribute.tldr: MAPLE combines prompts for histological structures and whole slides with cross-scale graph learning to improve few-shot pathology classification.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can write code for machine learning tasks, but their choices may be limited by their existing knowledge and broad changes to entire implementations. MLE-STAR addresses both issues. It starts by searching the web for effective models relevant to the task, using this external information to construct an initial solution.

The agent then improves selected parts of the solution through repeated, targeted exploration. Ablation studies analyze the contribution of individual code blocks and guide where to focus further work. This supports deeper investigation of specific components, such as feature engineering, instead of making every iteration a complete redesign. The authors also introduce an ensembling method based on a strategy suggested by MLE-STAR.

On MLE-bench, the method earns medals in 64% of the evaluated Kaggle competitions, significantly exceeding the best alternative reported in the abstract. The result supports a workflow that combines external model discovery with evidence-guided local refinement. Its central contribution is organizing automated machine learning engineering around informed starting points and focused experimentation.
neurips-2025-mle-star-machine-learning-e.tldr: MLE-STAR combines web-based model discovery with ablation-guided component refinement, earning medals in 64% of MLE-bench competitions.

paragraphs: Models that analyze individual video frames can recognize objects and motion while producing predictions that disagree in three-dimensional space. These inconsistencies can appear as spatial misalignment or flickering over time. Motion4D brings information from two-dimensional foundation models into a shared, time-varying 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to improve geometric and semantic consistency.

Its optimization alternates between sequential stages that update motion and semantic fields and a global stage that jointly refines attributes for longer-term coherence. A 3D confidence map adjusts motion guidance dynamically. Adaptive resampling adds Gaussians where color or semantic errors indicate that the representation needs more coverage, directing additional capacity toward underrepresented regions.

Motion4D also alternates between refining semantic fields and updating SAM2 prompts to resolve inconsistent object interpretations. Evaluations report significant improvements over both 2D foundation models and existing 3D approaches on point tracking, video object segmentation, and novel-view synthesis. The results support coordinating motion, geometry, and semantics within one evolving representation rather than relying on independently consistent-looking frames.
neurips-2025-motion4d-learning-3d-consis.tldr: Motion4D integrates 2D model guidance into a dynamic 3D representation to improve consistency in motion, object semantics, and rendered views.

paragraphs: This paper studies how training can produce multi-step reasoning in transformers using a concrete symbolic problem: finding paths in trees. It considers backward reasoning, which traces a goal node to the root, and a harder forward task. The forward task first constructs that backward path and then reverses it to obtain the root-to-goal route.

The authors analyze gradient descent and prove that trained one-layer transformers can solve both tasks with guarantees for generalization to unseen trees. For forward reasoning, their analysis identifies multiple phases of learning. Different attention heads learn specialized roles and coordinate to carry out the two subtasks within a single autoregressive sequence.

The result provides a mechanistic account of learned sequential computation in this setting, connecting training dynamics with the eventual reasoning procedure. It also suggests that organizing tasks around intermediate chain-of-thought steps can allow shallow multi-head transformers to solve problems that would otherwise require deeper architectures. This architectural implication is tied to the structured reasoning setting studied, rather than a universal claim about all reasoning tasks.
neurips-2025-multi-head-transformers-pro.tldr: The paper proves that one-layer multi-head transformers trained by gradient descent can learn structured tree-path reasoning and generalize to unseen trees.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization in which the unknown is a probability distribution and the objective can be non-convex. A relative-entropy penalty keeps the distribution related to a fixed reference measure. The authors analyze Best Response flow, also called fictitious play flow, and related entropy-regularized min-max problems with neither convex nor concave structure.

The main question is how non-convexity, regularization strength, and the reference measure's tail behavior interact. The authors show how to choose the regularizer so that the Best Response operator contracts distances measured by the L1-Wasserstein metric. Under that construction, the operator has a unique fixed point, which they establish as the unique global minimizer of the regularized optimization problem.

The result extends earlier convex analyses by allowing non-convex objectives in exchange for a specific regularizer choice. It does not claim the same guarantee for arbitrary regularization. The authors also demonstrate applications to policy optimization in Markov decision processes and Markov games with softmax policies in the mean-field regime, connecting the theory to reinforcement learning.
neurips-2025-non-convex-entropic-mean-fi.tldr: A carefully chosen entropy regularizer makes Best Response optimization contractive for certain non-convex distributional objectives, yielding a unique global minimizer.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network often means highlighting influential nodes or subgraphs. Such highlights can show where relevant information lies without explaining how it supports the prediction. This paper investigates logical rules as a more explicit description of the decision process, focusing on explanations produced within the model's own learning architecture.

The proposed model, LogiX-GIN, incorporates logic layers into a graph neural network. These layers generate interpretable rules as part of learning, linking the explanation to the computations used for prediction. This addresses a gap in existing logic-based approaches, which the abstract describes as predominantly post-hoc analyses focused on graph classification.

Across several graph-based tasks, LogiX-GIN achieves competitive predictive performance while providing clear logical explanations. The authors characterize these explanations as faithful and aligned with the model's internal operations. The contribution is therefore an architecture that combines graph prediction and rule-based explanation within the same process, with experiments supporting the possibility of retaining useful predictive performance alongside this form of interpretability.
neurips-2025-on-logic-based-self-explain.tldr: LogiX-GIN embeds logic layers in a graph neural network so its predictions come with rules aligned with its internal computations.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression at locations within tissue. Clustering these locations into coherent regions helps reveal tissue organization. Existing approaches combine expression measurements with spatial information, but often leave out biological information encoded in the DNA sequences of the expressed genes. SAINT adds this sequence information to the clustering representation.

The authors construct sequence-augmented data for fourteen tissue sections across DLPFC, HBC, and MBA benchmarks. They retrieve reference DNA sequences for expressed genes and encode them with a pretrained Nucleotide Transformer. For each spatial spot, expression-weighted and attention-based pooling combine gene embeddings into a spot-level sequence representation, which is then fused with the spatial-expression representation.

Experiments show consistent clustering improvements across multiple datasets and examine the framework's effectiveness, sensitivity, and transferability. These results support the complementary value of sequence-derived features: they add useful information alongside where genes are expressed and how strongly they are expressed. The contribution is a unified integration method that makes sequence-level biological priors available to spatial clustering.
neurips-2025-saint-sequence-aware-integr.tldr: SAINT improves spatial transcriptomics clustering by combining DNA-sequence embeddings with gene-expression and spatial representations.

paragraphs: An agent's sequence of reasoning and tool interactions contains feedback about how it approached a task. SE-Agent treats these complete trajectories as material for further improvement. The paper argues that existing search approaches can underuse relationships between trajectories, leading to repeated reasoning and insufficient diversity in the solution paths being explored.

The framework revisits earlier pilot trajectories through revision, recombination, and refinement. These operations use previous attempts to guide new ones and allow ideas from separate trajectories to inform each other. The intended benefit is a wider search beyond local optima, together with reduced influence from unproductive reasoning paths. Improvement happens through iterative optimization of the agent's problem-solving process.

The authors evaluate SE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified, where agents resolve real GitHub issues, using five strong language models. They report gains of up to 55% relative improvement and state-of-the-art performance among open-source agents on that benchmark. The result supports reusing and combining information across attempts as an effective way to improve multi-step software problem solving.
neurips-2025-se-agent-self-evolution-tra.tldr: SE-Agent revises, combines, and refines previous interaction trajectories to improve multi-step reasoning and software issue resolution.

paragraphs: Software security tasks involve repositories, reproducible failures, and ambiguity that simplified challenges may not capture. SEC-bench introduces an automated framework for evaluating language-model agents on authentic security engineering work. Its contribution includes both the construction of reproducible benchmark instances and an evaluation of agents on two practical task types.

A multi-agent scaffold assembles code repositories with testing harnesses, reproduces vulnerabilities in isolated environments, and produces reference patches for evaluation. The authors report a construction cost of $0.87 per instance. They use the resulting data to test proof-of-concept generation, which demonstrates a vulnerability, and vulnerability patching, which attempts to fix the underlying problem.

On the complete dataset, evaluated state-of-the-art coding agents achieve success rates of at most 18.0% for proof-of-concept generation and 34.0% for patching. These results expose substantial gaps on the tested security tasks. The automated construction process also offers a way to create evaluations grounded in reproducible software artifacts, making the observed successes and failures tied to concrete engineering outcomes.
neurips-2025-sec-bench-automated-benchma.tldr: SEC-bench automatically builds reproducible security tasks and finds low success rates among evaluated agents on vulnerability demonstration and patching.

paragraphs: In two-player zero-sum stochastic games with perfect information, different optimality criteria capture increasingly fine distinctions between strategies. Mean-payoff optimality concerns long-run average reward. Blackwell optimality requires a strategy to remain optimal for every discount factor sufficiently close to one. The intermediate notion of d-sensitive optimality connects these two ends of the hierarchy.

The paper studies discount thresholds above which every strategy optimal for the discounted game is guaranteed to satisfy the relevant stronger criterion. These thresholds matter computationally because solving a sufficiently patient discounted game provides a route to finding such strategies. The stated iteration bound grows as the reciprocal of one minus the discount factor, making proximity to one consequential for computation.

The authors give the first bounds for d-sensitive thresholds beyond the mean-payoff case and improve existing Blackwell threshold bounds. Their analysis uses separation bounds for algebraic numbers, including Lagrange bounds, Mahler measures, and multiplicity theorems. The contribution is a sharper mathematical basis for reducing these refined strategy-selection problems to discounted games.
neurips-2025-thresholds-for-sensitive-op.tldr: The paper bounds discount thresholds that make discounted-game solutions satisfy stronger long-run optimality criteria in stochastic games.

paragraphs: Poisoning attacks in federated learning manipulate training so the shared model misclassifies attacker-chosen inputs. Training-time defenses aim to prevent this outcome, but the paper reports limited effectiveness when client data distributions differ greatly or many clients are malicious. FLForensics addresses what happens after such defenses fail and a poisoned model has been deployed.

The method starts when a misclassified target input is identified and aims to trace the attack back to the responsible clients. Its role is therefore forensic and complementary to prevention. It asks which participants caused the poisoning, using the discovered target failure as the starting point for attributing the attack.

The authors theoretically show that FLForensics can distinguish benign from malicious clients under their formal definition of a poisoning attack. They also evaluate existing and adaptive attacks across five benchmark datasets and report effective tracing. Together, these results support post-attack attribution as an additional defense capability, with the theoretical claim tied to the paper's specified attack definition.
neurips-2025-tracing-back-the-malicious-.tldr: FLForensics traces federated-learning poisoning attacks back to malicious clients after a target misclassification has been discovered.

paragraphs: During reinforcement fine-tuning, a multimodal model's reasoning patterns can change in ways that either improve adaptation or introduce harmful bias. This paper studies detrimental concept drift in chain-of-thought reasoning, especially for chest diagnosis. It formalizes autoregressive reasoning tokens as non-stationary distributions subject to arbitrary temporal changes, linking concept drift theory with reinforcement fine-tuning.

The proposed Counterfactual Preference Optimization method uses language-model experts supported by concept graphs to generate counterfactual reasoning trajectories. These trajectories help distinguish useful adaptation from harmful shifts in reasoning. Counterfactual-aware preference alignment then guides custom tuning, with the aim of making reinforcement fine-tuning more stable as the reasoning distribution changes.

Experiments report improvements in robustness, generalization, and coordination within reinforcement fine-tuning. The authors also contribute CXR-CounterFact, containing 320,416 curated counterfactual reasoning trajectories derived from MIMIC-CXR. The work combines a theoretical description of changing reasoning distributions, an optimization method for responding to those changes, and a dataset supporting the counterfactual approach in the medical setting.
neurips-2025-walking-the-tightrope-auton.tldr: Counterfactual Preference Optimization uses alternative reasoning trajectories to separate useful adaptation from harmful reasoning drift during reinforcement fine-tuning.

paragraphs: When external rewards are rare, reinforcement-learning agents need other signals to decide what to explore. Curiosity can supply such a signal, but surprising observations may reflect randomness rather than useful discovery. In multi-agent environments, treating every surprise equally can also overlook informative changes in other agents' behavior and the task dynamics they reveal.

CERMIC adjusts intrinsic curiosity using inferred multi-agent context. It filters noisy surprise signals and calibrates exploration based on information about peers, targeting decentralized settings without communication. Its theoretically grounded intrinsic rewards encourage transitions with high information gain. The aim is to direct exploration toward experiences that improve understanding of the environment rather than simply produce unexpected observations.

The authors evaluate CERMIC on VMAS, Meltingpot, and SMACv2, reporting significant improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms in sparse-reward environments. These empirical results support contextual calibration as a useful component of multi-agent exploration. The central idea is that curiosity becomes more informative when it accounts for both environmental noise and what other agents' behavior reveals.
neurips-2025-wonder-wins-ways-curiosity-.tldr: CERMIC improves sparse-reward multi-agent exploration by filtering noisy surprise and adjusting curiosity using inferred peer context.
